Fast Cox Proportional Hazards Estimation for Two Groups

Source: R/coxph_fast.R
coxph_fast.Rd

Fits the Cox proportional hazards model with a single treatment indicator to a two-group parallel trial and returns the maximum partial likelihood estimate of the hazard ratio, the standard error of its logarithm, and a Wald-type confidence interval, using output names consistent with summary(survival::coxph(...)). The C++ backend forms the risk sets in a single pass over the pooled sorted data and runs the Newton-Raphson iteration on the numbers at risk and of events at the distinct event times, so that an iteration takes time in proportion to the number of distinct event times rather than the number of subjects.

Usage

coxph_fast(
  time,
  event,
  group,
  control,
  side = 2,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  presorted = FALSE,
  strata = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  ties = c("efron", "breslow")
)

Arguments

time

A numeric vector of follow-up times for all subjects (pooled over both groups). Alternatively, a formula Surv(time, event) ~ group, optionally with strata() terms, with the variables in data; see formula_interface.

event

An integer or numeric vector of event indicators (1 = event, 0 = censored), aligned with time.

group

A vector of group labels aligned with time. Any type that supports equality comparison is accepted.

control

A scalar value indicating which level of group represents the control group. Subjects with group != control are treated as the treatment group. With the formula interface it defaults to the first level of the group variable.

side

1 for a one-sided test in the direction of treatment benefit (hazard ratio below 1, i.e. a negative coefficient) or 2 for a two-sided test (default 2). The returned vector has no p-value: side is stored as an attribute, and the print() method reports the p-value that follows it. The confidence interval is always two-sided at conf.level.

conf.level

A single numeric value in (0, 1) specifying the confidence level for the Wald interval. Defaults to 0.95.

presorted

A logical value. If TRUE, time, event, and group are assumed to be already sorted in ascending order of time (with strata, sorted by stratum and by time within stratum, so that the rows of each stratum are contiguous), and the internal order() call is skipped. If FALSE (default), sorting is handled internally. The order is checked, and an error is given when it does not hold.

strata

An optional vector of stratum labels aligned with time, without missing values. When supplied, the stratified estimator described in Details is computed. Several stratification factors can be combined with interaction(). NULL (default) gives the unstratified estimator.

data

A data frame in which the variables of a formula given as time are evaluated. Used only with the formula interface; see formula_interface.

ties

A character string naming the handling of tied event times, "efron" (default, as in survival::coxph()) or "breslow". Without tied event times the two give the same result.

Value

An object of class "coxph_fast", which is a named numeric vector of length 5 with elements matching the column names of summary(coxph(...))$coefficients and summary(coxph(...))$conf.int:

coef

Estimate of the log hazard ratio.

exp(coef)

Estimate of the hazard ratio.

se(coef)

Standard error of coef, from the observed information at the estimate.

lower .95

Lower bound of the Wald confidence interval for the hazard ratio. The label reflects conf.level (e.g., "lower .90" when conf.level = 0.90).

upper .95

Upper bound of the Wald confidence interval.

The attributes ties, iter (the number of Newton-Raphson iterations), and converged record the fit. With strata, the number of strata is stored in the attribute strata. The elements are NA_real_ (still with class "coxph_fast") when the estimate cannot be computed (no events, or an infinite estimate as described in Details), with converged = NA, and when the iteration does not converge in 20 iterations, with converged = FALSE and a warning. The object also has the class "fastsurv", whose as.data.frame(), coef(), and confint() methods are described in as.data.frame.fastsurv.

Details

Let t_k (k = 1, ..., K) denote the distinct observed event times in the pooled sample. At each t_k, let n_T_k and n_C_k be the numbers at risk in the treatment and control groups just before t_k (subjects censored at t_k are at risk at t_k), and let O_T_k, O_C_k, and O_k = O_T_k + O_C_k be the numbers of events in the treatment group, in the control group, and in total at t_k. With the log hazard ratio beta and r = exp(beta), the log partial likelihood of Cox (1972) with the Breslow (1974) handling of tied event times is

l(beta) = sum_k [O_T_k beta - O_k log(n_C_k + n_T_k r)].

The Efron (1977) handling treats the O_k tied events at t_k as occurring one after another and replaces the k-th term by O_T_k beta minus the sum, over m = 0, ..., O_k - 1, of log(n_C_k + n_T_k r - (m / O_k) (O_C_k + O_T_k r)). Without tied event times the two coincide. With strata, the risk sets are formed within each stratum and l(beta) is the sum over strata, so that the hazard ratio is common to all strata and each stratum has its own baseline hazard.

The estimate maximizes l(beta) by Newton-Raphson iteration from beta = 0, which Therneau and Grambsch (2000, Appendix E) work through on a small data set. A step after which l(beta) decreases is halved. From the first halved step on, the iteration also keeps the interval between the largest value at which the score l'(beta) has been found positive and the smallest value at which it has been found negative, and a trial value outside this interval is replaced by its midpoint; this keeps the iteration convergent when the hazard ratio is extreme and one group is small. The iteration stops when the relative change in l(beta) is at most 1e-9, and at most 20 iterations are taken. The starting value, the convergence criterion, and the maximum number of iterations are those of survival::coxph() with the default coxph.control(), so that the two estimates agree to rounding error when no step is halved; when a step is halved, they can differ within the convergence tolerance.

The standard error of the log hazard ratio is 1 / sqrt(I), where I = -l”(beta) is the observed information at the estimate, and the Wald confidence interval for the hazard ratio is exp(coef -/+ z * se(coef)), where z is the standard normal quantile for conf.level.

Let O_T be the total number of events in the treatment group, L the number of events at times when no control subject is at risk, and H the number of events at times when a treatment-group subject is at risk. The score decreases in beta, from O_T - L as beta tends to -Inf to O_T - H as beta tends to Inf, so the estimate is finite if and only if L < O_T < H. Otherwise (for example, when all events are in one group) the estimate is infinite and the result is NA, whereas survival::coxph() returns a large finite value, usually with a warning.

Times are tied only when they are exactly equal. By default survival::coxph() also treats as tied the times that differ only by rounding error (timefix = TRUE in coxph.control()); the two give the same result when no distinct times are that close, and coxph.control(timefix = FALSE) gives the comparable fit otherwise.

The returned object has class "coxph_fast" and is a named numeric vector of length 5. A print() method formats the result similarly to summary(coxph(...)).

References

Breslow, N. (1974). Covariance analysis of censored survival data. Biometrics, 30(1), 89-99.

Cox, D. R. (1972). Regression models and life-tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Methodological), 34(2), 187-202.

Efron, B. (1977). The efficiency of Cox's likelihood function for censored data. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 72(359), 557-565.

Therneau, T. M., & Grambsch, P. M. (2000). Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox Model. New York: Springer.

See also

coxph for the Cox model with any covariates. print.coxph_fast for the print method.

Examples

library(survival)

# Compare coxph_fast with coxph on the ovarian dataset.
# coxph() treats rx as numeric with rx = 1 as the reference (control),
# so set control = 1 for a consistent comparison.
fit_fast <- coxph_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx, control = 1)
fit_fast
#> Cox proportional hazards model for two groups
#> 
#>   control = 1
#>   ties = efron
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>          coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> group -0.5964    0.5508   0.5870 -1.016     0.31
#> 
#> Hazard ratio and 95% Wald confidence interval:
#>       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> group    0.5508     1.8155    0.1743    1.7404

fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian)
c(coxph_fast = unname(fit_fast["coef"]), coxph = unname(coef(fit_cox)))
#> coxph_fast      coxph 
#>   -0.59638   -0.59638 
c(coxph_fast = unname(fit_fast["se(coef)"]),
  coxph = sqrt(fit_cox$var[1, 1]))
#> coxph_fast      coxph 
#>  0.5869895  0.5869895 

# The Breslow handling of tied event times
coxph_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx, control = 1,
           ties = "breslow")
#> Cox proportional hazards model for two groups
#> 
#>   control = 1
#>   ties = breslow
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>          coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> group -0.5964    0.5508   0.5870 -1.016     0.31
#> 
#> Hazard ratio and 95% Wald confidence interval:
#>       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> group    0.5508     1.8155    0.1743    1.7404

# Stratified by residual disease, compared with coxph(... + strata())
coxph_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx, control = 1,
           strata = ovarian$resid.ds)
#> Stratified Cox proportional hazards model for two groups (2 strata)
#> 
#>   control = 1
#>   ties = efron
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>          coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> group -0.6626    0.5155   0.5955 -1.113    0.266
#> 
#> Hazard ratio and 95% Wald confidence interval:
#>       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> group    0.5155     1.9399    0.1605    1.6562
coef(coxph(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx + strata(resid.ds), data = ovarian))
#>        rx 
#> -0.662632 

# presorted = TRUE: sort once outside, reuse inside a loop
ord <- order(ovarian$futime)
coxph_fast(ovarian$futime[ord], ovarian$fustat[ord], ovarian$rx[ord],
           control = 1, presorted = TRUE)
#> Cox proportional hazards model for two groups
#> 
#>   control = 1
#>   ties = efron
#>   alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>          coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
#> group -0.5964    0.5508   0.5870 -1.016     0.31
#> 
#> Hazard ratio and 95% Wald confidence interval:
#>       exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> group    0.5508     1.8155    0.1743    1.7404

# Formula interface, and the result as a data frame (log hazard ratio)
fit_f <- coxph_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian)
as.data.frame(fit_f)
#>   term estimate std.error  conf.low conf.high statistic   p.value
#> 1 coef -0.59638 0.5869895 -1.746858 0.5540983 -1.015998 0.3096304
exp(confint(fit_f))
#>          2.5 %   97.5 %
#> coef 0.1743207 1.740371

# \donttest{
# Speed comparison against coxph()
if (requireNamespace("microbenchmark", quietly = TRUE)) {
  microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
    coxph_fast = coxph_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx, 1),
    coxph      = coxph(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian),
    times = 1000
  )
}
#> Unit: microseconds
#>        expr     min       lq      mean  median       uq      max neval cld
#>  coxph_fast  33.030  38.0665  46.44389  48.162  53.2345  119.538  1000  a 
#>       coxph 730.139 759.4925 805.48657 769.427 783.0880 5444.940  1000   b
# }
